hypothesis: Trimethylamine-N-oxide reductase (cytochrome c; K07811, torZ/torY-type, EC 1.7.2.3) gene abundance is increased or characteristic in the fecal metagenome of 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: I found no study that directly measured K07811 (torZ/torY-type TMAO reductase, EC 1.7.2.3) abundance in infant fecal metagenomes comparing an early complementary-feeding timepoint (~4-6 months) with ~12 months, so there is no direct feature+group evidence. What exists is indirect and partly conflicting. Supporting the hypothesis: (i) respiratory TMAO reductase systems (torCAD, torYZ) are essentially restricted to facultatively anaerobic Gammaproteobacteria, and human-gut TMAO-to-TMA reduction has been attributed experimentally to Enterobacteriaceae (Escherichia, Klebsiella); (ii) genome-resolved metagenomics of an early infant gut community showed TMAO/DMSO/nitrate reductase genes carried by the E. coli-dominated population, i.e. these alternative-electron-acceptor respiration genes are a hallmark of the immature, Proteobacteria-rich gut; (iii) multiple longitudinal/cross-sectional infant cohorts (including one sampling exactly 4, 9 and 12 months during complementary feeding) report that Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance falls markedly across the second half of the first year as obligate anaerobes (Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes) expand, which would mechanically lower the community-level abundance of Enterobacteriaceae-encoded TMAO reductase by 12 months. Counterweighting this: KEGG places K07811 in the 'methane metabolism' map, and several infant studies report that methane-metabolism/methanogenesis and nitrogen-metabolism gene categories are *higher* after introduction of solids and in non-human-milk-fed infants, and a first-year longitudinal metagenome/archaeome study described methane-related pathways becoming more prominent at 12 months; additionally, serum TMAO (the substrate for this enzyme) increased from 5 to 12 months in meat-fed infants, so substrate-driven induction at 12 months is plausible. Because nothing addresses this specific gene in this specific age contrast and the pathway-level signals point in opposite directions, this is weak, mixed evidence (score 1) rather than moderate support or contradiction.

evidence.title: Metabolic retroconversion of trimethylamine N-oxide and the gut microbiota
evidence.study_population: C57BL/6J mice fed deuterated TMAO plus in vitro human/animal gut bacterial isolates and communities
evidence.relevance: Primary experimental evidence that gut microbial reduction of TMAO to TMA is carried out predominantly by Gammaproteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae (TMAO reductase activity), establishing which taxa carry the K07811-type function in the gut; indirect support because these taxa are enriched in early infancy.

evidence.title: Genome resolved analysis of a premature infant gut microbial community reveals a Varibaculum cambriense genome and a shift towards fermentation-based metabolism during the third week of life
evidence.study_population: Premature human infant, longitudinal genome-resolved fecal metagenomics in the first weeks of life
evidence.relevance: Directly documents TMAO reductase (along with fumarate, DMSO, nitrate/nitrite reductase) genes in the early infant gut community, largely attributable to E. coli, i.e. this respiratory capacity is a feature of the young, Proteobacteria-dominated infant microbiome; also reports a shift away from respiration toward fermentation as the community matures.

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Healthy US infants sampled at ~4, 9 and 12 months (shotgun metagenomics + LC-MS metabolomics), 'Nourish to Flourish' pilot
evidence.relevance: Age-matched to this contrast: reports that most Proteobacteria (which carry torCAD/torYZ TMAO reductases) decrease in relative abundance between 4 and 9 months, being replaced by Firmicutes - indirect support for higher TMAO-reductase gene abundance at ~5 months than 12 months. Notes overall functional gene profiles change less than taxonomy, a caveat for KO-level predictions.

evidence.title: Evolution of the Gut Microbiome in Early Childhood: A Cross-Sectional Study of Chinese Children
evidence.study_population: Cross-sectional cohort of Chinese children from birth to 36 months
evidence.relevance: Shows a significant, progressive decline in Proteobacteria relative abundance from birth through 24 months, supporting the expectation that Enterobacteriaceae-encoded functions such as TMAO reductase decline between 5 and 12 months of age.

evidence.title: Age-associated gut microbiome succession, colonization resistance, and relative resistome patterns in an antibiotic-restricted infant cohort
evidence.study_population: Antibiotic-restricted infant cohort, stool sampled at ~1 and 6 months
evidence.relevance: Quantifies the age-related decline of Enterobacteriaceae (median 16.6% at 1 month to 1.9% at 6 months) with concurrent expansion of obligate anaerobes; indirect, taxon-level support for a downward trajectory of Enterobacteriaceae-borne respiratory reductase genes with infant age (though the timepoints are earlier than 5 vs 12 months).

evidence.title: Trimethylamine N-Oxide - an overview (ScienceDirect Topics)
evidence.study_population: Review/encyclopedic synthesis of human and animal gut microbiota studies
evidence.relevance: Corroborates that Proteobacteria, especially Escherichia and Klebsiella spp., are the main contributors to TMAO-to-TMA conversion via the TMAO reductase pathway in the human gut - the taxonomic anchor for the hypothesis, but review-level rather than primary.

contradicting_evidence: Pathway-level infant evidence points the other way for the KEGG category this KO is filed under: a longitudinal infant study using 16S+PICRUSt reported that energy-metabolism genes, specifically nitrogen and methane metabolism, were overrepresented in infants after introduction of solid foods compared with exclusively breastfed infants (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4318912/; summarized also in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9633281/), and a first-year oral/gut anaerobic microbiome-archaeome study described the 12-month (M12) metagenome shifting toward more complex metabolism 'down to methane' relative to 6 months (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/msystems.01071-24). In addition, quantitative TMAO - the substrate that induces tor operon expression - increased from 5 to 12 months in infants on a meat-based complementary diet (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7912106/), which could favor higher TMAO-reductase capacity at 12 months. None of these measured K07811 itself, so they are suggestive rather than a direct refutation, which is why the score is 1 (mixed/indirect) rather than -1.

caveats: No primary study located reports K07811/torZ/torY (or EC 1.7.2.3) gene abundance for 5-month vs 12-month infant stool, so all support is inferential from (a) the taxonomic ownership of TMAO reductase by Enterobacteriaceae and (b) the well-documented decline of Enterobacteriaceae/Proteobacteria across the first year. KO-level abundance need not track phylum-level abundance, and the complementary-feeding metagenomic study explicitly found functional gene profiles change far less than taxonomy over 4-12 months. K07811's KEGG assignment to 'methane metabolism' means pathway-level results for methane/methanogenesis in infants (which trend upward with solid foods) are not a valid proxy for this specific enzyme in either direction. Formula- vs breast-fed status, delivery mode, and antibiotic exposure are strong confounders of Enterobacteriaceae abundance and hence of this gene, and none of the cited cohorts were designed around the 5- vs 12-month contrast in formula-fed infants specifically.
